html.body: Date: 2025-01-28 REMARKSClaims 1-10 were previously canceled. Claims 11-30 are currently pending. Claims 11, 14, 19, 20, 29, and 30 are currently amended. The amendments submitted on December 12, 2024 were not entered, therefore, they are again submitted here with additional new amendments.Advisory Action The Advisory Action maintains that Chahine describes generating and sensing a signal, and Chen describes repeating a protocol.The claims require first "generating of the controller-generated signal" and then, next "sensing of the controller-generated signalusing the another textile-based ECG electrode pairing." Thus, a signal is controller-generated, and then, next, that controller-generated signal is detected.For the reasons discussed below, the Advisory Action does not show how the Office contends that Chahine teaches the foregoing feature as claimed in the context of the claimed subject matter, and therefore, it would not have been obvious to "repeat the claimed protocol" as alleged by the Office Action.A. Chahine Is Not Shown to Disclose Sensing a Controller-Generated Signal As recited by claim 1, the controller-generated signal is "generated by a controller device" and is not a signal that is generated by a patient's physiological signals naturally produced by the body as part of its biological functions, e.g., bioelectric signals originating from the heart (ECG), brain (EEG), or muscles (EMG).Chahine, in the asserted portions, describes that the conductive fabric patch is used as both a sensor and as an electrode as required (e.g. to sense body signals or information about the body, and then to provide stimulation in response to those signals). Chahine generally describes the functionality of its sensing electrodes as being capable of detecting "body signals or information about the body," but the Office has not shown that sensing such "body signals or information about the body" is sensing a "controller-generated signal." If this assertion is repeated, Applicant respectfully requests Office to show how even under the broadest reasonable interpretation standard that sensing "body signals or information about the body" is sensing a "controller-generated signal." B. The Cited Electrical Stimulations are Not Sensed Chahine generates an electrical stimulation that causes "repeated muscular contraction" of a muscle positioned proximate to or underlying the electrode. Cited paragraph [0004] explains that electronic stimulation devices deliver impulses through electrodes to "mimic the action potentials coming from the central nervous system thereby causing the muscles to contract." This clearly identifies the electrodes as stimulation electrodes. The electrodes are described as being placed on the skin "in direct proximity to muscles and/or nerves to be stimulated," emphasizing their role in delivering stimulation.Similarly, cited paragraph [0151] focuses on the design and functionality of stimulation electrodes, particularly in the context of delivering electrical stimulation through EMS (Electrical Muscle Stimulation), TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation), or ENS (Early Neurological Stimulation) elements. The cited paragraph describes that the design and dimensions (e.g., cross-sectional area, width, length) of the EMS/TENS/ENS elements can control "the effectiveness and amount of electrical stimulation generated" in specific regions.The present claims generate the controller-generated signal and then sense the controller- generated signal. In contrast, Chahine generates a stimulation after sensing body signals.Because Chahine is not shown to teach these limitations, it would not have been obvious to repeat the claimed process as suggested by the Office Action.35 USC 103 Claims 11-16, 18-23, and 25-30 are rejected as being unpatentable over Chahine et al. (US 2017/0056644) in view of Chen et al. (US 2010/0041975).1. Chen does not teach or suggest "repeat said generating the controller-generated signal and said sensing of the controller-generated signal using the another textile-based ECG electrode pairing" as recited by amended claims 11 and 29.The present claims require "repeat said generating of the controller-generated signal and said sensing of the controller-generated signalusing the another textile-based ECG electrode pairing." The Office Action, at page 5, acknowledges that this limitation is not taught by Chahine.However, the Office Action cites Chen para. [0045] - [0046] as teaching this limitation.Chen, paragraph 0045 describes the functionality of the system, which includes identifying electrodes and avoiding premature switching by allowing adequate time for circuitry stabilization. It also mentions that the system checks signal quality (i.e., at most every four seconds).Chen, paragraphs 0046 describes considerations for signal quality, such as electrode-skin contact and electrode placement across the heart.However, none of these paragraphs, nor the remainder of Chen, describe repeating said generating the controller-generated signal and sensing of the controller-generated signal as recited by the present claims.By overlooking the generation of the controller-generated signal by the controller device, the Office Action improperly dissects the claim and focuses only on isolated elements, ignoring the role of the controller device, contrary to the principle that claims must be considered as a whole. As stated in MPEP § 2141.02: "In determining the differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious." At least for this reason, claims 11 and 29 are considered to be patentable over the cited art.2. Chen does not teach or suggest "based on the sensing the controller-generated signal generated by the controller device ... deselect the at least one determined textile-based ECG electrode from the electrode pairing, and select another textile-based ECG electrode pairing, repeat said generate and said sense of the controller-generated signal using the another textile-based ECG electrode pairing" as recited by amended claims 11 and 29.Claim 11 as amended requires certain steps in response to sensing the controller-generated signal generated by the controller device. In particular, deselecting the ECG electrode pairing, selecting another ECG electrode pairing, and repeating the process of generating and sensing the controller-generated signal using the another electrode pairing. As discussed above, Chen does not have a controller-generated signal generated by a controller device, and therefore, fails to teach the claimed ECG electrode pairing.Instead, Chen describes "generate physiological data derived from the electrical signals." This is data coming from the patient, not from a controller device.At least for this reason, claims 11 and 29 are considered to be patentable over the cited art.CONCLUSIONRecognizing that Internet communications are not secure, I hereby authorize the USPTO to communicate with the undersigned and practitioners in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33 and 37 CFR 1.34 concerning any subject matter of this application by video conferencing, instant messaging, or electronic mail. I understand that a copy of these communications will be made of record in the application file.Applicant believes that a one-month extension of time is necessary. In the event that an extension is needed, this conditional petition of extension is hereby submitted. Applicant requests that deposit account number 14-1449 be charged for any fees that may be required for the timely consideration of this application.Date: January 28, 2025 Respectfully submitted, /Emmanuel D.
